# Blaise Pascal quote sources

8 passages attributed to Blaise Pascal in this archive, each with the locator that lets you find it in the work itself — and the one thing that most often goes wrong when people quote Pascal.

[Quote source](https://www.philosophydef.com/quote-source) / Blaise Pascal

How to cite this author, and what circulates under the name that is not theirs to give.

## Sourcing profile

Language of the works

French

Cited here from

The Pensées, cited by fragment number in the Brunschvicg scheme, and passages from the Lettres provinciales elsewhere in the corpus.

How to cite it

Fragment number plus the numbering scheme — Brunschvicg, Lafuma, or Sellier. This is not pedantry: the schemes number the fragments differently, so “§200” in one edition is not the fragment that holds the same sentence in another.

Where quotations of this author go wrong

The Pensées is not a book. Pascal died in 1662 with the material in bundles of papers, and it was assembled and numbered by editors over three centuries. So a Pensées citation always cites an editorial arrangement as well as an author, and the same thought can sit at two different numbers in two standard editions.

1 of the passages below have been worked through against the cited edition, with the original-language wording and the circulating variants recorded on their own pages.

## Frequently asked questions

### Where can I check quotations attributed to Blaise Pascal?

Fragment number plus the numbering scheme — Brunschvicg, Lafuma, or Sellier. This is not pedantry: the schemes number the fragments differently, so “§200” in one edition is not the fragment that holds the same sentence in another. This archive cites Blaise Pascal from The Pensées, cited by fragment number in the Brunschvicg scheme, and passages from the Lettres provinciales elsewhere in the corpus. Every passage listed on this page carries that locator, so it can be found in any edition of the work.

### What is the most common mistake when quoting Blaise Pascal?

The Pensées is not a book. Pascal died in 1662 with the material in bundles of papers, and it was assembled and numbered by editors over three centuries. So a Pensées citation always cites an editorial arrangement as well as an author, and the same thought can sit at two different numbers in two standard editions.

### What language did Blaise Pascal write in?

French. Any English sentence you read is a translation, so a complete source names the translator as well as the passage.
